Option B: Twentieth century topic

text: How far were criticisms of the Freedmen’s Bureau valid?
Study the Background Information and the sources carefully, and then answer all parts of
Question 1.
Background Information
The Freedmen’s Bureau was established by Congress in 1865. It was meant to help freed
people achieve economic security and political rights. It issued rations and clothing and operated
hospitals and schools. It also supervised labour contracts between planters and freed people.
However, it had many critics. They claimed that its work was hampered by incompetent and
corrupt agents. White Southerners, who were determined to keep freed people poor and
powerless, claimed it created useless jobs for Republicans and it made black Americans lazy. In
January 1866, Congress passed a bill renewing the Bureau’s charter, but in the following month
President Johnson vetoed the bill. In April, Johnson sent Generals Steedman and Fullerton to the
South to find evidence to discredit the Bureau. Congress finally passed the bill in July.
Was the criticism of the Freedmen’s Bureau fair?
Source A
The Freedmen’s Bureau is the nation’s right arm, gently but firmly outstretched to keep the
peace between the warring classes. Its main aims are to save the blacks from famine, abuse and
massacre, to set them to work and to see that they are well treated and fairly paid for their labour.
It has achieved a marvellous success. Hundreds of thousands of blacks who are now hard
working and comfortable labourers, with a roof over their heads and food in their cabins, would
have been thieving and starving without the Bureau.
From the New York Tribune newspaper, February 1866. The Tribune was owned by
Horace Greeley, who was a Radical Republican at that time.
Source B
The bill to renew the charter of the Bureau ought to be called an act to support the blacks in
idleness by the honest labours of white people, or an act to establish a gigantic and corrupt
political machine for the benefit of the Radicals. The supposed aim of the bill, to protect and
benefit the freedmen, cannot be achieved by legislation. On the contrary, it will destroy their
independence of character and action by making them dependent on government. Never
prepared to work more than they had to, and having always been taught to rely on others,
they are naturally idle, dependent and useless to themselves. How can the planters and other
employers use these people as labourers, when the corruption of the thousands of Bureau
agents stands in the way? Why should we be burdened with a charitable institution to support the
African Americans at the cost of many millions a year?
From the New York Herald newspaper, February 1866. The Herald supported the
Democratic Party.

Source C
The labourer on the plantation is in the clutches of his employer. If he is mistreated, where can
he go for help? He has nowhere. If he goes to the Freedmen’s Bureau agent, he finds there an
officer who rides, dines and drinks champagne with his employer. Most of the agents think their
job is to provide the planters with cheap workers, and to keep the labourers on the plantations.
They are, in fact, the planters’ guards. It is, therefore, useless for the poor labourer to look to the
Bureau for help. He knows that the Bureau will send him back to his unjust employer. He will not
be assisted to get his pay, but will be told to go back to his master and do his work.
From the New Orleans Tribune, the first daily newspaper for black Americans, October 1867.
Source D
There are different opinions over whether the Bureau encourages habits of hard work or idleness
among the freedmen. In those districts where the Bureau is run by men of sound judgement,
there has been no conflict between the Bureau and the local citizens. Officers of the Bureau
have helped the rights of freedmen, such as the right to hold property. But in many places a very
unsatisfactory situation exists. Bureau agents employ freedmen on their own plantations and pay
them a low rate of wages, thus giving government support to levels of wages far below what the
labour is really worth.
The idle and worthless look to the Bureau for support. The mass of freedmen have the idea that
the Bureau is there to serve them and that if they do not have the standard of living they require,
they can fall back on the Bureau for support. They also regard the existence of the Bureau as
evidence that the government looks upon white people of the South as their enemies, which
causes bad feeling.
From the Report of Generals Steedman and Fullerton, who visited Southern states.
The report was published in May 1866.
Source E
The final report of Generals Steedman and Fullerton has been made public. Their predictable
conclusion is that the Bureau is a nuisance, and is served by unworthy agents and that its
continuance will produce disagreement and oppression. These Presidential fault-finders accuse
the Bureau of re-enslaving the freedmen by contracts which impose wages far below what they
should be. The very success of the Bureau in restoring labour and increasing the value of the
labourer, is turned against it as a crime when it is doing its best to encourage industry, security,
good morals and justice among all classes of the population. On evidence that is one-sided and
inconclusive, and with hostile motives, the report supports the President’s message.
From The Nation newspaper, August 1866. The Nation was published in New York.

text: How far did the Germans have good reason for being angry about the Treaty of Versailles?
Study the Background Information and the sources carefully, and then answer all parts of
Question 2.
Background Information
The peace terms agreed by the Allies were presented to the German delegation on 7 May 1919.
The Germans had two weeks to respond. Both the German delegation and people in Germany
were shocked by the terms, which included loss of territory, the war guilt clause, reparations and
disarmament. By the end of May, Germany had responded with its objections. Minor changes
were made to the terms but the substance of the Treaty was unchanged. The Germans were told
to sign the Treaty and, on 28 June, they did so very reluctantly.
Were the Germans justified in their claims that the Treaty was unfair?
Source A
Once the Germans agreed to the Armistice, they thought that they would be consulted on
the Treaty, but this was not the case and caused them to regard the Treaty as a ‘Diktat’. The
Treaty of Versailles included little of Wilson’s ideas. One of the most controversial terms of the
Treaty was the War Guilt Clause, which blamed Germany for the war. This was unfair and led
to Germany being forced to disarm and pay reparations, which it could not afford, to the Allied
powers. In a clumsy rearrangement of the map of Europe, the Treaty broke up and redistributed
the German empire and unsurprisingly contributed to German resentment in the period after the
war. Most objectionable and hated were the arrangements for Germany’s eastern frontiers and
the revival of Poland. Although Wilson was opposed to such harsh terms, he was outmanoeuvred
by Clemenceau, who aimed at weakening Germany as much as possible.
From a recent study of the Treaty of Versailles.
Source B
Unsurprisingly, the Germans were not included in the negotiations for the Treaty. It is not true
to say that the Treaty was lacking in idealism. Much was achieved at Versailles and the Treaty
bears Wilson’s mark. The new map of Europe was drawn according to the principle of self-
determination. The new frontiers were Wilsonian and ensured that only three per cent of the total
population of Europe lived under foreign rule. No previous frontiers had been so satisfactory.
On the economic side the Treaty was too harsh. The reparations were too high and harmed the
stability of the new regime in Germany but the Germans most hated being unjustly blamed for
the war. However, many in France thought that Clemenceau had failed and had left Germany too
strong for the future peace of the world.
From a recent account of the Treaty of Versailles.

Source E
After the loss of its colonies and merchant fleet, Germany will no longer be in a position to import
raw materials in sufficient quantities. An enormous part of German industry will be condemned
to extinction and it will no longer be able to provide bread and work for millions of people. The
enforcement of the Peace Treaty will lead to the deaths of several million people. This will occur
soon because the health of the population has been broken by the starvation blockade. The
Peace will impose on Germany many times the number of deaths caused by the war. Those
who sign this Treaty will be responsible for the deaths of many millions of German men, women
and children.
The German reply to the proposed Treaty, 15 May 1919.

Source F
The reparations to be levied on Germany may be difficult to defend, but they were based by the
Allies on Germany’s own prosperity. Don’t let us allow ourselves to be deceived by the protest
and outcry that comes from Germany. While France’s industrial machinery was ruthlessly
destroyed by Germany, Germany’s factories are still intact. Germany’s aggression in starting the
war resulted in enormous damage. The total cost of the war to the world has been set at not less
than $348 billion. Therefore, when the Allies now propose that Germany should pay a sum which
amounts to only about $13 billion, it does not seem unreasonable. Germany, with a population
twice as large as France – skilful, able, industrious, with its industrial machinery unharmed –
should be able to pay this amount. Do not let us forget that during the war Germany was happily
announcing that it would be able to make the Allies pay $500 billion.
From an article by Thomas William Lamont, one of Wilson’s chief advisors at the
peace conference, 1921.
Source G
The historian, with every justification, will come to the conclusion that we were very stupid
men. We arrived in Paris as fervent followers of President Wilson and determined that a peace
of justice and wisdom should be negotiated. We left, conscious that the Treaties imposed on
our enemies were neither just nor wise. Those who wish to see the gap between intention and
practice should read the notes to the Conference by the German delegation. It is impossible to
read the German criticism without forming the impression that the Peace Conference was guilty
of disguising an imperialistic peace under the cloak of Wilsonism. Seldom has such a desire for
revenge been hidden by such deceit.
From a book by Harold Nicolson, a member of the British delegation at Versailles,
published in 1933.
